2027-03-13.title: Fifth Saturday of the Great Fast
2027-03-13.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Love is the greatest of all
2027-03-13.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-13.verse: Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
theo: We usually hear the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians at weddings, and it belongs there. But Paul did not write it for a bride and groom. He wrote it for a quarrelsome parish in a rich port city, where believers competed over spiritual gifts, divided into parties, and went to court against one another. So he begins by emptying every gift of its value if love is missing: “If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.” Even heroic giving counts for nothing without it. Then he describes love not with feelings but with verbs, things love does and does not do: “Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices in the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.” An old retreat preacher used to tell his listeners to read these lines again, putting their own name in place of the word love, and to stop at the first line where it became untrue. Only one Name fits every line: Jesus. Corinth was famous for its bronze mirrors, which gave back a blurred and darkened image; Paul uses them for our present knowledge of God: “For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then we will see face to face.” Prophecies, tongues and knowledge will pass; “And now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.”

In the Gospel some Pharisees test Jesus with a question much debated among the teachers of his day: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” Jesus asks what Moses commanded, and they answer that Moses allowed a certificate of dismissal. Jesus goes back further than Moses, to the beginning: “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote this commandment for you. But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” The Church has kept this word faithfully: a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, cannot be dissolved by any human power. This is not a heavy burden laid on weak shoulders; it is a gift of grace, for Christ who asks it gives the strength to live it. At a Syro-Malabar wedding the bridegroom ties the minnu around the bride's neck and places the manthrakodi upon her, both blessed by the priest, signs of a bond meant to last until death. Paul's hymn is the daily bread of such a marriage: patient, kind, not irritable, bearing and enduring all things. At the same time the Church does not forget those whose marriages have been wounded or broken. They remain her children, are welcome in the parish, are accompanied with care, and may seek the help of the Church's tribunals to examine whether a true marriage existed. The Great Fast is a good time for every married couple to renew their promise, and for every family to pray for the marriages that are struggling.
outline: Ask: if I put my name in place of love, where does the sentence become untrue?
Gifts, knowledge and sacrifice emptied of value.
Point 2 · Love is patient, love is kind
The verbs of love in daily life.
Marriage from the beginning, and grace to live it.
“Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”
live: Read 1 Corinthians 13 with your name (1 Corinthians 13:4)
Read verses 4 to 7 slowly, putting your own name in place of love, and choose the one line you will practise today.
If you are married, pray tonight with your spouse for your marriage; if not, pray for a couple you know who are struggling.
2027-03-13.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the love that is patient and kind, that bears all things and never ends. Without you we are noisy gongs and clanging cymbals. Make us patient and kind in our homes; strengthen husbands and wives to remain one flesh, as God joined them from the beginning; heal the wounds of broken marriages and console those who suffer from them; and bring us all at last from the dim mirror to see you face to face. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana Christ, the Bridegroom, gives himself to the Church his bride; every Christian marriage draws from this altar the love that never ends.

quick: Paul: without love every gift is nothing; love is patient, kind, and never ends.
Jesus: from the beginning God made them one flesh; what God has joined, let no one separate.
Faith, hope and love abide, and the greatest of these is love.
2027-03-13.action: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 with your own name in place of love, and practise one line today.
2027-03-13.question: Is my love patient and kind at home, where it is hardest?

family.explain: Paul tells us what real love looks like. Love is patient: it waits. Love is kind: it helps. Love is not jealous, not proud, not rude. Love does not always want its own way. Love does not get angry quickly and does not keep count of wrongs. When Mummy and Pappa love each other like this, and when we love one another like this, our home becomes a little piece of heaven.
family.intention: We pray for all married couples, especially for those who are having difficulties.
family.ask: Ask: “Which line of this reading is hardest for our family? Let us practise it this week.”

illus: On their fiftieth wedding anniversary in a parish near Irinjalakuda, an old couple was asked by their grandchildren for the secret of a long marriage. The husband joked that he had learned to say only two words: Yes, dear. His wife laughed, and then said more seriously: we had many bad days. On the worst of them we still knelt together for the family prayer, even when we were not speaking to each other. Sometimes the Our Father was the only sentence we said to each other all day. But we said it together, and in the morning we started again.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are love itself. Fill our hearts and our homes with your patient and kind love as we pray. Amen.
share: If I do not have love, I am nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2). Where am I doing good things without love?
Love is patient; love is kind (1 Corinthians 13:4). Who at home most needs my patience and kindness?
What God has joined together, let no one separate (Mark 10:9). How can I support the marriages in my family and parish?
interc: For the Church, the Bride of Christ, that she may be faithful in love.
For married couples, that they may grow in patient and kind love.
For couples whose marriages are wounded or broken, and for their children.
For young people preparing for marriage.
For our group, that our love may be shown in deeds.
pm.close: Father, you made man and woman in your image and joined them as one flesh. Pour your love into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, strengthen every marriage and family, and lead us to see you face to face. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Paul tells a divided parish in Corinth: if I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal (1 Corinthians 13:1). Without love, every gift is nothing.

Love is patient; love is kind; it does not insist on its own way; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). Put your own name in place of love, and see where you must grow this Lent.

In the Gospel Jesus goes back to the beginning: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate (Mark 10:6–9). Christian marriage is a gift of grace, and Christ gives the strength to live it.

Let us pray today for all married couples, especially those who are struggling, and for those whose marriages are broken, who remain our brothers and sisters. Faith, hope and love abide, and the greatest of these is love (1 Corinthians 13:13). Amen.
kids: Children, Paul says that love is patient and kind, and does not always want its own way. Can you be patient and kind with your brothers, sisters and parents today, even when it is hard?

intro: Theme: “Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”
Love without which every gift is nothing, the patient and kind love of daily life, and the marriage that God joined from the beginning.

q: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. If one offered for love all the wealth of one's house, it would be utterly scorned.
If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.
points.apply: Do one good work today simply out of love, expecting nothing in return.

q: Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
points.apply: Pray tonight for your own marriage, or for a marriage you know that is struggling.

q: One thing I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: to live in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to inquire in his temple.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then we will see face to face. Now I know only in part; then I will know fully, even as I have been fully known.
points.apply: Spend ten minutes before the Blessed Sacrament this week, asking to see the Lord's face more clearly.

concl: Without love we are nothing; with Christ's love a home becomes a sanctuary.
What God has joined, his grace can keep; and the love we practise now will see him face to face.
2027-03-13.resolve: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 each evening this week with your own name, and pray for the marriages in your family.
